Head coach | highlights = * [[NFL Comeback Player of the Year]] (2010) * 4× [[Pro Bowl]] ([[2003 Pro Bowl|2002]], [[2005 Pro Bowl|2004]], [[2006 Pro Bowl|2005]], [[2011 Pro Bowl|2010]]) * [[Bert Bell Award]] (2010) * [[Touchdown Club of Columbus#Archie Griffin Award|Archie Griffin Award]] (1999) * First-team [[College Football All-America Team|All-American]] ([[1999 College Football All-America Team|1999]]) * [[Big East Conference football individual awards#Offensive Player of the Year|Big East Offensive Player of the Year]] (1999) * [[Big East Conference football individual awards#Rookie of the Year|Big East Rookie of the Year]] (1999) ;NFL records * Career [[yards per carry]] (minimum 750 career rushing attempts): 7.0 | statlabel1 = [[Passing attempts]] | statvalue1 = 3,217 | statlabel2 = [[Passing completions]] | statvalue2 = 1,807 | statlabel3 = [[Completion percentage]] | statvalue3 = 56.2% | statlabel4 = [[Touchdowns|TD]]–[[Interceptions|INT]] | statvalue4 = 133–88 | statlabel5 = [[Passing yards]] | statvalue5 = 22,464 | statlabel6 = [[Passer rating]] | statvalue6 = 80.4 | statlabel7 = [[Rushing yards]] | statvalue7 = 6,109 | statlabel8 = [[Touchdown|Rushing touchdowns]] | statvalue8 = 36 | regular_record = {{Winning percentage|1|11|record=y}} | playoff_record = {{Winning percentage|0|0|record=y}} | overall_record = {{Winning percentage|1|11|record=y}} | pfr = V/VickMi00 | CollegeHOF = 2558 }} '''Michael Dwayne Vick''' (born June 26, 1980) is an American [[college football]] coach and former professional football player who is the [[head coach]] for the [[Norfolk State Spartans football|Norfolk State Spartans]]. He played in the [[National Football League]] (NFL) for 13 seasons and was the all-time leader in quarterback rushing yards at the time of his retirement. Vick played [[college football]] at [[Virginia Tech]], winning the [[Touchdown Club of Columbus#Archie Griffin Award|Archie Griffin Award]] as a freshman, and was selected [[List of first overall National Football League draft picks|first overall]] by the [[Atlanta Falcons]] in the [[2001 NFL draft]]. During his six years with the Falcons, he was named to three [[Pro Bowl]]s and led the team to two playoff runs, one division title, and an [[NFC Championship Game]] appearance. Vick's NFL career broke off in 2007 after he pleaded guilty for his [[Bad Newz Kennels dog fighting investigation|involvement in a dog fighting ring]] and spent 21 months in federal prison. His arrest and subsequent conviction garnered Vick notoriety with the general public, which lasted throughout the rest of his career. He was released by the Falcons shortly before leaving prison. After serving his sentence, Vick signed with the [[Philadelphia Eagles]] for the 2009 season. As a member of the Eagles for five years, he had his greatest statistical season and led the team to a division title in 2010, earning him [[NFL Comeback Player of the Year|Comeback Player of the Year]] and a fourth Pro Bowl selection. In his final two seasons, Vick played for the [[New York Jets]] and [[Pittsburgh Steelers]], primarily as a backup. He officially retired in 2017 after spending the 2016 season as a free agent. After retiring as a player, Vick pursued a coaching career. He served as an advisor for the [[Atlanta Legends]] of the [[Alliance of American Football]] (AAF) in 2019. Near the end of the 2024 season, Vick was named the head football coach at [[Norfolk State University|Norfolk State]].

'''Michael Anthony Strahan''' ({{IPAc-en|ˈ|s|t|r|eɪ|h|æ|n}} {{Respell|STRAY|han}}; born November 21, 1971)<ref name=biography.com>{{cite web|url=https://www.biography.com/athlete/michael-strahan|title=Michael Strahan (1971–)|publisher=[[Biography.com]]|access-date=March 11, 2020|archive-date=March 11, 2020|archive-url=https://archive.today/20200311181948/https://www.biography.com/athlete/michael-strahan|url-status=live}}</ref> is an American television host and former professional [[American football|football]] [[defensive end]] who played in the [[National Football League]] (NFL) for 15 seasons with the [[New York Giants]]. A dominant pass rusher, Strahan set the NFL single-season record for [[quarterback sack]]s and helped the Giants win [[Super Bowl XLII]] in his final season in 2007. He was inducted into the [[Pro Football Hall of Fame]] in 2014.

Upon retirement from the NFL, Strahan became a media personality. He appears as a football analyst on ''[[Fox NFL Sunday]]'', and served as a co-host of [[American Broadcasting Company|ABC]]'s ''[[Good Morning America]]'' as well as ''[[Live with Kelly and Mark|Live! with Kelly and Michael]]'' with [[Kelly Ripa]] from 2012 to 2016, for which he won two [[Daytime Emmy Award]]s. He has also made guest appearances on game shows and other programs. In 2014, he became a regular contributor on ''Good Morning America'', and in 2016 the network announced that Strahan would be leaving ''Live!'' to join ''GMA'' full-time. He also hosts the current incarnation of the ''[[Pyramid (franchise)|Pyramid]]'' game show for ABC.

Strahan flew on a suborbital space flight on December 11, 2021, aboard the [[Blue Origin NS-19]]. At {{convert|6|ft|5|in}}, he became the tallest person to fly in space.

<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-1992-09-09-sp-279-story.html|title = Archives|website = [[Los Angeles Times]]}}</ref>

'''Michael Charles Smith Jr.''' (born November 21, 1970) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player who was a [[wide receiver]] for the [[Kansas City Chiefs]] of the [[National Football League]] (NFL). He played [[college football]] for the [[Kansas State Wildcats football|Kansas State Wildcats]].

Born in 1970 in [[New Orleans]], Smith attended Jesuit High School in that city. He played [[college football]] at [[Kansas State University]] from 1988 to 1991.<ref name=PFA/> He set all-time Kansas State receiving records with 179 receptions in 43 games for 2,457 yards and 11 receiving touchdowns.<ref>{{cite news|title=Smith and Hernandez|newspaper=The Mercury|date=November 24, 1991|page=B8|url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/the-mercury-smith-and-hernandez/167262148/}}</ref> He received third-team All-America honors in both 1990 and 1991.<ref>{{cite news|title=Smith honored|newspaper=The Mercury|date=November 22, 1990|page=9|url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/the-mercury-smith/167264099/|via=[[Newspapers.com]]}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|title=Football News names Smith to third team|newspaper=The Mercury|date=June 20, 1991|page=9|url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/the-mercury-smith/167262785/|via=[[Newspapers.com]]}}</ref> He also played professional football in the NFL for the [[Kansas City Chiefs]] in 1992, appearing in two games.<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/players/S/SmitMi20.htm | title=Michael Smith stats |access-date=March 4, 2025 |publisher=Pro-Football-Reference.com}}</ref><ref name=PFA>{{Cite web |title=Michael Smith |url=https://profootballarchives.com/players/s/smit28200.html |access-date=March 4, 2025 |work=Pro Football Archives}}</ref>
